extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (or beginners) studying sentential logic / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook guidance for analyzing, translating, and manipulating sentential (propositional) formulas: forming well‑formed formulas, building truth tables, testing validity, using equivalences, and working with variables and truth sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-formed formulas (WFF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strings such as P ∧/∨ Q, P¬Q, P¬ ∧ Q are 'ungrammatical' in the language of logic; grammatical expressions are called well‑formed formulas or formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only certain combinations of symbols constitute meaningful formulas. Operators ∧ and ∨ are used between two statements; ¬ is used before a statement. Examples of well-formed formulas appear in the text; ungrammatical examples include P¬ ∧ Q, P ∧/∨ Q, and P¬Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connective usage constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbols ∧ and ∨ can only be used between two statements (to form conjunctions/disjunctions), and ¬ only before a statement (to negate it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to algebraic operators: +, −, ·, ÷ used between numbers and unary − used before a number. Violating these positional rules yields meaningless expressions. When forming formulas, ensure each connective is placed with appropriate operand(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate by meaning, not word-by-word
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the logical form of an English sentence you must think about what the sentence means rather than just translating word for word into symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words like 'but' and 'and' can sometimes express disjunction (e.g., 'Rain and snow are the only two possibilities' means 'either rain or snow'). Analyze the semantic role of the natural-language words before mapping to ∧, ∨, ¬.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize hidden logical structure in mathematical notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical notations may hide logical connectives; e.g., 3 ≤ π is (3 < π) ∨ (3 = π), and 3 ≤ π < 4 is [(3 < π) ∨ (3 = π)] ∧ (π < 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading compound mathematical inequalities or symbols, expand them into their logical components to reveal embedded ∧/∨ structure. You may sometimes omit substituting letters when substatements are short, writing (3 < π) ∨ (3 = π) or simply (3 ≤ π).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct truth tables systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: List all possible combinations of truth values for the propositional letters; if a formula contains n different letters its truth table will have 2^n lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order the rows systematically to avoid skipping possibilities. For each complex formula, work from component parts up to the whole formula, computing columns stepwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of ∨ (inclusive vs exclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, ∨ means inclusive or (P or Q, or both) unless specified otherwise; exclusive or is a different connective (often denoted +).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making truth tables or translating English, treat ∨ as inclusive by default. If the intended meaning is 'but not both', use exclusive or notation or an equivalent formula built from ∧, ∨, ¬.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stepwise truth-table computation and main connective
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute truth values for component parts step by step (starting from letters), and identify the main connective under which the final truth values are listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can either compute separate columns for intermediate subformulas or use the compact method of listing truth values beneath the corresponding connective symbols in the original formula. The symbol under which the final truth values appear is the formula's main connective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity criterion via truth tables
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument is valid if the premises cannot all be true while the conclusion is false; verify this by examining rows of the truth table where all premises are true and checking the conclusion's truth value in those rows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a truth table including columns for all premises and the conclusion. Find any row where every premise is true but the conclusion is false — if any such row exists, the argument is invalid; otherwise it is valid. Examples in the text demonstrate locating counterexample rows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence and substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Two formulas are equivalent if they have the same truth values in every possible valuation; equivalent formulas can be substituted for one another in any expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth tables to test equivalence. Once equivalence is established, you may replace complicated subformulas with simpler equivalents to simplify reasoning or check validity. Examples show (¬S ∧ L) ∨ S equivalent to L ∨ S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common logical equivalence laws (know and apply)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be familiar with standard equivalences: DeMorgan’s laws, commutative, associative, idempotent, distributive, absorption, and double negation laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists these laws explicitly (e.g., ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q; P ∧ Q ≡ Q ∧ P; P ∧ (Q ∨ R) ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R); ¬¬P ≡ P, etc.). These laws may be applied to subformulas (letters may be replaced by any formulas) and combined to derive more complex simplifications. Use them instead of brute-force truth tables where convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses optionality via associativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of associative laws, parentheses may be omitted in long conjunctions/disjunctions (e.g., P ∧ Q ∧ R) without ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associative equivalences justify leaving out parentheses when combining three or more statements with the same connective; ensure you only omit parentheses when associativity applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tautologies and contradictions (definitions and manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tautology is a formula that is always true; a contradiction is always false. Examples: P ∨ ¬P is a tautology; P ∧ ¬P is a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth tables to check whether a formula is a tautology/contradiction. Apply tautology/contradiction laws in simplifications (e.g., P ∧ (a tautology) ≡ P; ¬(a tautology) is a contradiction). Recognize and exploit tautologies/contradictions to simplify formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic-style simplification of formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply equivalence laws (distributive, associative, idempotent, DeMorgan, double negation, absorption, tautology/contradiction laws) step by step to find simpler formulas equivalent to a given formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides worked examples (e.g., ¬(P ∨ ¬Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ Q; ¬(Q ∧ ¬P) ∨ P ≡ ¬Q ∨ P). When simplifying, justify each step by naming the law used. This often reveals why an argument is valid/invalid without checking every truth-table row.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact truth-table technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of separate columns for each subformula, list truth values below the corresponding connective symbol in the original formula and compute upward to the main connective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This compact method reduces clutter and still enforces the stepwise computation of component truth values. The final values under the main connective match those you'd obtain with full columnar tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-builder notation and elementhood tests ({x | P(x)})
rubrics_metrics.description: A set can be defined by an elementhood test: B = {x | x is a prime number} means the elements of B are exactly the values of x that make the statement 'x is a prime number' true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit elementhood tests rather than ambiguous ellipses when defining infinite or large sets. Treat statements used in {x | P(x)} as tests: y ∈ {x | P(x)} is equivalent to P(y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth set of a statement P(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth set of P(x) is the set of all values of x that make P(x) true: Truth set of P(x) = {x | P(x)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth sets to describe which variable values satisfy a property. This notion is defined here for statements with one free variable; later chapters extend it to multiple free variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free vs bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Free variables stand for objects the statement says something about; bound variables are dummy variables used inside notations (such as {x | ...}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bound variable may be renamed without changing meaning (e.g., {x | x^2 < 9} and {w | w^2 < 9}). In expressions like y ∈ {x | x^2 < 9}, y is free and x is bound; y ∈ {x | x^2 < 9} is equivalent to y^2 < 9. Determine which variables are free to know whether the statement's truth depends on variable values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and counterexamples to diagnose invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: When an argument appears invalid, a truth-table row demonstrating premises true and conclusion false pinpoints the problematic valuation; examples illuminate why the inference fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook uses specific arguments to show how to read off invalidity (e.g., (¬S ∧ L) ∨ S with S yields a counterexample row where both S and L true). Use the truth table to find the exact condition causing invalidity (e.g., both S and L true).

rubrics_metrics.name: Care in translating English to logic with multiple variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When statements mention objects and relations, use predicate-like notation with variables and argument order mattering (e.g., M(x) for 'x is a man', L(x,y) for 'x likes y'), and capture relationships precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer using predicate notation P(x), D(y,x) etc., to preserve the dependency between variables rather than flattening to propositional letters that lose structure. Explicit variable ordering matters (e.g., L(x,y) ≠ L(y,x)).
